title: خِتَامُ حِكَايَةِ الْقَرَنْدَلِيِّ الثَّانِي وَبِدَايَةُ حِكَايَةِ الْقَرَنْدَلِيِّ الثَّالِثِ
titleEn: The End of the Second Qalandar's Tale, and the Beginning of the Third's
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 98–105 (continuing directly from nights-13, whose text breaks off as the Second Qalandar recites his sentence of the shapeshifting duel), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the project’s own two-pass-plus-adjudication pipeline; the edition’s own OCR is unusable. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition’s — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm exactly as Macnaghten prints it. Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms and its occasional compositor’s slips, is preserved unaltered; a few genuinely obscure or corrupt-looking forms are vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes rather than silently repaired. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized automatically once this file is published, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 14 finishes the Second Qalandar’s tale and opens the Third’s. The princess and the returning efrit Jirjīs fight out their duel through a chain of paired transformations — lion and serpent, scorpion and eagle, black bird and parti-colored wolf, pomegranate seed and rooster — until a stray seed becomes a fish, the rooster a whale, and both efrit and princess burst into flame, the fire scarring the king, killing a eunuch, and finally consuming them both; the princess dies confessing the shahāda, having forgotten to swallow the one seed that held the efrit’s life. The king mourns her seven days, entombs her ashes under a dome, falls gravely ill, then on recovering bitterly dismisses the disenchanted young man (the tale’s narrator) from the kingdom — grieving, but absolving him of intent. Shaved, one-eyed and in mourning felt, the young man wanders to Baghdad, arriving the same night he meets his companion the First Qalandar and, moments later, the Third, all three strangers brought by chance to this same door. The Third Qalandar then opens his own tale, “stranger and more amazing” than the others’: a seafaring king’s pleasure voyage among nearby islands runs into a storm, a stretch of uncanny water, and a lookout’s sighting of something dark on the horizon — the legendary Black, or Magnetic, Mountain, crowned with a bronze horseman-and-horse automaton whose fall is the fleet’s only hope. The ships are drawn in and torn apart nail by nail; the king alone survives, washed onto the mountain’s foot, and finds a stair cut into its face just as dawn cuts Shahrazad off. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularized the language here and there, so some of the original Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit. The night is frank about violence (the mutilation of the princess and the young man, the mass drowning of the fleet) and is translated that way, without euphemism.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الرَّابِعَةَ عَشَرَ قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ اَنْقَرَنْدَلِي قَالَ لِلصَّبِيَّةِ يَا سِتِّي
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-rābiʿata ʿashara qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna anqarandalī qāla li-al-ṣabiyyati yā sittī
sentences.l: Now when it was the fourteenth night, she said: It has reached me, O happy King, that Anqarandalī said to the girl, "O my lady,"
sentences.i: Now when the fourteenth night came, she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Anqarandalī said to the girl, "My lady..."
sentences.n: The archive prints ان انقرندلي as two words, an أَنَّ (the complementizer required after بلغني) followed by a name-like word اَنْقَرَنْدَلِي, kept here letter for letter as an unanalyzed proper name rather than reparsed into القرندلي ('the Qalandar', the narrator of this frame-tale, which is what the context otherwise suggests). سِتِّي is the colloquial contraction of سَيِّدَتِي, 'my lady/mistress'.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ بِنْتَ الْمَلِكِ أَخَذَتْ يَدَهَا سِكِّينًا مَكْتُوبٌ عَلَيْهَا بِالْأَسْمَاءِ الْعِبْرَانِيَّةِ وَخَطَّتْ بِهَا دَائِرَةً وَسَطَ الْقَصْرِ
sentences.tr: thumma inna binta al-maliki akhadhat yadahā sikkīnan maktūbun ʿalayhā bi-al-asmāʼi al-ʿibrāniyyati wa-khaṭṭat bihā dāʼiratan wasaṭa al-qaṣri
sentences.l: Then the daughter of the king took, her hand, a knife, written upon which (were) the Hebrew names, and she drew with it a circle (in) the middle of the palace,
sentences.i: Then the king's daughter took up in her hand a knife inscribed with the Hebrew Names, and with it drew a circle in the middle of the palace,
sentences.n: يَدَها stands where classical usage would have بِيَدِها ('with her hand'); Middle Arabic here drops the preposition before the instrumental noun, a pattern that recurs below.

sentences.t: وَكَتَبَتْ عَلَيْهَا أَسْمَاءً وَطِلَّسْمَاتٍ وَعَزَمَتْ وَقَرَأَتْ بِكَلَامٍ يُفْهَمُ وَكَلَامٍ لَا يُفْهَمُ
sentences.tr: wa-katabat ʿalayhā asmāʼan wa-ṭillasmātin wa-ʿazamat wa-qaraʼat bi-kalāmin yufhamu wa-kalāmin lā yufhamu
sentences.l: and she wrote upon it names and talismans, and she conjured, and she recited with speech understood and speech not understood.
sentences.i: and wrote upon it names and talismans, and pronounced her adjurations, reciting words that could be understood and words that could not.
sentences.n: عَزَمَتْ is used absolutely in the technical sense of performing an exorcistic/magical adjuration, not merely 'she resolved'.

sentences.t: فَبَعْدَ سَاعَةٍ أَظْلَمَتْ عَلَيْنَا الدُّنْيَا وَإِذَا بِالْعِفْرِيتِ قَدْ تَلَا عَلَيْنَا فِي صِفَتِهِ وَهَيْئَتِهِ لَهُ أَيْدٍ كَالْمَدَارِي وَأَرْحُلٌ كَالسَّوَارِي وَعَيْنَيْنِ مِثْلَ شُعَلِ النَّارِ
sentences.tr: fa-baʿda sāʿatin aẕlamat ʿalaynā al-dunyā wa-idhā bi-al-ʿifrīti qad talā ʿalaynā fī ṣifatihi wa-hayʼatihi lahu aydin ka-al-madārī wa-arḥulun ka-al-sawārī wa-ʿaynayni mithla shuʿali al-nāri
sentences.l: Then after an hour the world grew dark upon us, and behold, the efrit had come upon us in his description and his shape: to him (were) hands like winnowing-forks, and legs like columns, and two eyes like the flames of fire.
sentences.i: Then after a while the world went dark around us, and suddenly the efrit loomed over us in his true form: he had hands like great forks, legs like pillars, and eyes like blazing fire.
sentences.n: تَلَا ('followed/recited') is an odd verb for an efrit's appearing; later in this same scene the text uses طَلَعَ ('rose up, appeared') for the same kind of event, so تلا here is likely a variant or slip for that sense — rendered contextually as 'loomed/appeared'. أَرْحُلٌ ('packs, mounts') is printed where the stock formula elsewhere has أَرْجُل ('legs'); kept as printed (ح not ج) and read by context as 'legs'. عَيْنَيْنِ uses the oblique dual form though the position is nominative — a common Middle Arabic leveling of the dual case, flagged here and not repeated below.

sentences.t: فَفَزِعْنَا مِنْهُ فَقَالَتْ بِنْتُ الْمَلِكِ لَا أَهْلًا بِكَ وَلَا سَهْلًا
sentences.tr: fa-faziʿnā minhu fa-qālat bintu al-maliki lā ahlan bika wa-lā sahlan
sentences.l: So we were frightened of him, and the daughter of the king said, "Neither family (welcome) to you, nor ease."
sentences.i: We were terrified of him, and the princess said, "No welcome to you, and no ease!"
sentences.n: She inverts the standard greeting أَهْلًا وَسَهْلًا ('welcome', literally 'family and ease') into its negation as a taunt.

sentences.t: فَاِنْقَلَبَ الْعِفْرِيتُ فِي صُورَةِ أَسَدٍ وَقَالَ لَهَا يَا خَائِنَةُ نَقَضْتِ الْعَهْدَ وَالْيَمِينَ أَ مَا تَحَالَفْنَا بِأَنْ لَا أَحَدَ مِنَّا يَتَعَرَّضُ لِلْآخَرِ
sentences.tr: fa-inqalaba al-ʿifrītu fī ṣūrati asadin wa-qāla lahā yā khāʼinatu naqaḑti al-ʿahda wa-al-yamīna amā taḥālafnā bi-an lā aḥada minnā yataʿarraḑu li-al-ākhari
sentences.l: So the efrit turned into the form of a lion, and said to her, "O traitress, you have broken the covenant and the oath — did we not swear together that no one of us would molest the other?"
sentences.i: The efrit turned into the shape of a lion and said to her, "You traitor! You have broken our covenant and our oath — did we not swear to each other that neither of us would harm the other?"
sentences.n: The archive prints an isolated ا between واليمين and ما ("واليمين ا ما تحالفنا"); read here, per the surprise-question sense, as أَمَا ('did ... not?'), a common rhetorical opener. If that stray mark is instead a page artifact rather than a hamza-alif, it can simply be dropped; the sense is the same either way.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ يَا لَعِينُ وَمِثْلُكَ لَهُ عِنْدِي يَمِينٌ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu yā laʿīnu wa-mithluka lahu ʿindī yamīnun
sentences.l: So she said to him, "O cursed one, and (does) the like of you have, with me, an oath?"
sentences.i: She said to him, "You cursed thing — does someone like you deserve an oath from me?"

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْعِفْرِيتُ خُذِي مَا جَاكِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-ʿifrītu khudhī mā jāki
sentences.l: So the efrit said, "Take what has come-to-you."
sentences.i: The efrit said, "Then take what's coming to you!"
sentences.n: جَاكِ is a contracted colloquial form of جَاءَكِ ('it came to you'), kept as printed rather than expanded to the classical form.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ فَتَحَ الْأَسَدُ فَمَهُ وَهَجَمَ عَلَى الصَّبِيَّةِ فَأَسْرَعَتْ وَأَخَذَتْ شَعْرَةً مِنْ شَعْرِهَا وَهَزَّتْهَا بِيَدِهَا وَهَمْهَمَتْ بِشَفَتَيْهَا فَصَارَتِ الشَّعْرَةُ سَيْفًا مَاضِيًا وَضَرَبَتْ بِهِ ذَلِكَ الْأَسَدَ فَصَارَ نِصْفَيْنِ وَاِنْقَلَبَتْ رَأْسُهُ عَقْرَبًا
sentences.tr: thumma fataḥa al-asadu famahu wa-hajama ʿalā al-ṣabiyyati fa-asraʿat wa-akhadhat shaʿratan min shaʿrihā wa-hazzathā bi-yadihā wa-hamhamat bi-shafatayhā fa-ṣārati al-shaʿratu sayfan māḑiyan wa-ḑarabat bihi dhālika al-asada fa-ṣāra niṣfayni wa-inqalabat raʼsuhu ʿaqraban
sentences.l: Then the lion opened his mouth and attacked the girl, so she hurried and took a hair from her hair, and shook it with her hand, and murmured with her lips, and the hair became a sharp sword, and she struck with it that lion, and he became two halves, and his head turned into a scorpion.
sentences.i: Then the lion opened his mouth and charged at the girl. She quickly plucked a hair from her head, shook it in her hand, and murmured under her breath, and the hair turned into a cutting sword. She struck the lion with it, so that he split into two halves, and his head turned into a scorpion.

sentences.t: فَاِنْقَلَبَتِ الصَّبِيَّةُ صَارَتْ حَيَّةً عَظِيمَةً وَهَمَّتْ عَلَى هَذَا اللَّعِينِ وَهُوَ فِي صِفَةِ عَقْرَبٍ فَتَقَاتَلَا قِتَالًا شَدِيدًا
sentences.tr: fa-inqalabati al-ṣabiyyatu ṣārat ḥayyatan ʿaẕīmatan wa-hammat ʿalā hādhā al-laʿīni wa-huwa fī ṣifati ʿaqrabin fa-taqātalā qitālan shadīdan
sentences.l: So the girl turned — became a huge serpent — and she set upon this cursed one, he being in the shape of a scorpion, and the two of them fought a fierce fight.
sentences.i: The girl transformed into a huge serpent and went for the cursed thing while it was in the shape of a scorpion, and the two of them fought a fierce battle.
sentences.n: انقلبت ... صارت stacks two verbs of becoming with no connective — a Middle Arabic habit of piling on synonymous verbs for emphasis, kept literally. هَمَّتْ عَلَى uses على where classical usage prefers هَمَّ بـ ('set about to'); the verb's government has shifted here.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ اِنْقَلَبَتِ الْعَقْرَبُ عُقَابًا فَاِنْقَلَبَتِ الْحَيَّةُ نِسْرًا وَصَارَتْ وَرَاءَ الْعُقَابِ وَطَلَبَتْهُ سَاعَةً زَمَانِيَّةً
sentences.tr: thumma inqalabati al-ʿaqrabu ʿuqāban fa-inqalabati al-ḥayyatu nisran wa-ṣārat warāʼa al-ʿuqābi wa-ṭalabathu sāʿatan zamāniyyatan
sentences.l: Then the scorpion turned into an eagle, and the serpent turned into a vulture, and she came (to be) behind the eagle and pursued him for a good while.
sentences.i: Then the scorpion turned into an eagle, and the serpent turned into a vulture, coming up behind the eagle and chasing it for a good while.
sentences.n: سَاعَةً زَمَانِيَّةً, literally 'an hour of time', is an idiom for 'a good while', used twice in this scene.

sentences.t: فَاِنْقَلَبَتِ الْعُقَابُ قَطًا أَسْوَدَ فَاِنْقَلَبَتِ الصَّبِيَّةُ ذِيبًا أَبْلَقَ فَتَقَاتَلَا فِي الْقَصْرِ سَاعَةً زَمَانِيَّةً
sentences.tr: fa-inqalabati al-ʿuqābu qaṭan aswada fa-inqalabati al-ṣabiyyatu dhiʼban ablaqa fa-taqātalā fī al-qaṣri sāʿatan zamāniyyatan
sentences.l: So the eagle turned into a black sand-grouse, and the girl turned into a piebald wolf, and the two of them fought in the palace for a good while.
sentences.i: The eagle turned into a black grouse, and the girl turned into a piebald wolf, and they fought together in the palace for a good while.

sentences.t: فَرَأَى الْقَطَٰ نَفْسَهُ مَغْلُوبًا فَاِنْقَلَبَ وَصَارَ رُمَّانَةً حَمْرَةً كَبِيرَةً وَقَعَدَتِ الرُّمَّانَةُ فِي وَسَطِ فِسْقِيَّةِ الْقَصْرِ
sentences.tr: fa-raʼā al-qaṭā nafsahu maghlūban fa-inqalaba wa-ṣāra rummānatan ḥamratan kabīratan wa-qaʿadati al-rummānatu fī wasaṭi fisqiyyati al-qaṣri
sentences.l: So the sand-grouse saw himself beaten, so he turned and became a large red pomegranate, and the pomegranate settled in the middle of the palace's pool.
sentences.i: Seeing himself beaten, the grouse turned into a large red pomegranate, which came to rest in the middle of the palace's ornamental pool.
sentences.n: القط is printed for القطا (the sand-grouse of the previous sentence), the final alif dropped just as قال is elsewhere printed قل; pointed here with a dagger alif over the ط to preserve the spelling while reading al-qaṭā. Here the archive's own فرأى already carries its hamza (unlike the bare فراى a few lines on, at P99L04); each is kept as printed. حَمْرَةً is the edition's spelling for classical حَمْرَاء ('red', fem.); kept as printed.

sentences.t: فَجَاءَ إِلَيْهَا الذِّيبُ فَاِرْتَفَعَتْ فِي الْهَوَاءِ وَوَقَعَتْ عَلَى بَلَاطِ الْقَصْرِ فَاِنْكَسَرَتْ وَاِنْتَشَرَ الْحَبُّ كُلُّ حَبَّةٍ وَحْدَهَا وَاِمْتَلَأَتْ أَرْضُ الْقَصْرِ حَبَّ رُمَّانٍ
sentences.tr: fa-jāʼa ilayhā al-dhību fa-irtafaʿat fī al-hawāʼi wa-waqaʿat ʿalā balāṭi al-qaṣri fa-inkasarat wa-intashara al-ḥabbu kullu ḥabbatin waḥdahā wa-imtalaʼat arḑu al-qaṣri ḥabba rummānin
sentences.l: Then the wolf came to it, and it rose up into the air and fell upon the pavement of the palace, and it broke, and the seed(s) scattered, every seed on its own, and the ground of the palace filled up with pomegranate-seed.
sentences.i: The wolf came toward it, so it shot up into the air and fell onto the palace's stone floor and shattered, scattering seeds every which way, until the whole palace floor was covered with pomegranate seeds.
sentences.n: الذِّيبُ is spelled throughout this passage with a plain ي and no hamza-seat, evidently the colloquial pronunciation dhīb rather than classical dhiʼb; kept as printed each time it recurs (also below).

sentences.t: فَاِنْتَفَضَ الذِّيبُ وَصَارَ دِيكًا وَاِلْتَقَطَ ذَلِكَ الْحَبَّ حَتَّى لَمْ يَتْرُكْ وَلَا حَبَّةً
sentences.tr: fa-intafaḑa al-dhību wa-ṣāra dīkan wa-iltaqaṭa dhālika al-ḥabba ḥattā lam yatruk wa-lā ḥabbatan
sentences.l: So the wolf shook himself and became a rooster, and picked up that seed until he left not even a single seed.
sentences.i: The wolf shook himself and turned into a rooster, and pecked up every one of those seeds until he had not left a single one.

sentences.t: فَبِالْأَمْرِ الْمُقَدَّرِ تَلَارَتْ حَبَّةٌ فِي جَانِبِ الْفِسْقِيَّةِ فَصَارَ الدِّيكُ يَصِيحُ وَيُرَفْرِفُ بِأَجْنِحَتِهِ وَيُشِيرُ إِلَيْنَا بِمِنْقَارِهِ وَنَحْنُ لَا نَفْهَمُ مَا يَقُولُ
sentences.tr: fa-bi-al-amri al-muqaddari talārat ḥabbatun fī jānibi al-fisqiyyati fa-ṣāra al-dīku yaṣīḥu wa-yurafrifu bi-ajniḥatihi wa-yushīru ilaynā bi-minqārihi wa-naḥnu lā nafhamu mā yaqūlu
sentences.l: But by the decreed matter, a seed تلارت beside the pool, so the rooster fell to crowing and flapping with his wings and pointing to us with his beak, while we did not understand what he was saying.
sentences.i: But as it was fated, one seed rolled out of reach by the edge of the pool, and the rooster began to crow and beat his wings and gesture at us with his beak, though we could not make out what he meant.
sentences.n: تَلَارَتْ is printed identically here and at P99L05 (checked against the page both times); it is not the expected تَدَارَتْ. The root is obscure — possibly a dialectal verb for 'rolled/slipped away' — kept exactly as printed; rendered by context as the seed getting out of the rooster's reach.

sentences.t: وَصَرَخَ عَلَيْنَا صَرْخَةً تَخَيَّلَ لَنَا أَنَّ الْقَصْرَ قَلْ اِنْقَلَبَ عَلَيْنَا وَدَارَ فِي أَرْضِ الْقَصْرِ كُلِّهِ فَرَأَى الْحَبَّةَ الَّتِي تَلَارَتْ فِي جَانِبِ الْفِسْقِيَّةِ فَاِنْقَضَّ عَلَيْهَا لِيَلْتَقِطَهَا
sentences.tr: wa-ṣarakha ʿalaynā ṣarkhatan takhayyala lanā anna al-qaṣra qad inqalaba ʿalaynā wa-dāra fī arḑi al-qaṣri kullihi fa-raʼā al-ḥabbata allatī talārat fī jānibi al-fisqiyyati fa-inqaḑḑa ʿalayhā li-yaltaqiṭahā
sentences.l: And he screamed at us a scream that made us imagine that the palace had turned over upon us, and it went spinning through the whole ground of the palace; then he saw the seed that had تلارت beside the pool, and swooped upon it to snatch it up.
sentences.i: He let out a scream that made us feel as if the palace itself had turned over on us, and it seemed to go spinning across the whole floor of the palace; then he spotted the seed that had rolled away by the pool and dove at it to snatch it up.
sentences.n: قَلْ here is the same letter-substitution misprint for قَدْ (ل for د) seen elsewhere in this scene (compare وَالْعِفْرِيتُ قَلْ صَرَخَ below, and تَقْلِرُ for تَقْدِرُ two sentences earlier) — 'that the palace had turned over upon us' reads far more naturally than treating the palace as speaking, so قَدْ is adopted here rather than قَالَ, matching the reading given to the same misprint elsewhere in this scene. Here فراى is printed bare (unlike the hamzated فرأى two sentences earlier), so its hamza is supplied.

sentences.t: وَإِذَا بِالْحَبَّةِ زَرَقَتْ فِي وَسَطِ الْمَاءِ الَّذِي فِي الْفِسْقِيَّةِ صَارَتْ سَمَكَةً وَغَارَتْ فِي قَعْرِ الْمَاءِ
sentences.tr: wa-idhā bi-al-ḥabbati zaraqat fī wasaṭi al-māʼi al-ladhī fī al-fisqiyyati ṣārat samakatan wa-ghārat fī qaʿri al-māʼi
sentences.l: And behold, the seed shot into the middle of the water that (was) in the pool — it became a fish and sank into the bottom of the water.
sentences.i: And suddenly the seed darted into the water of the pool, turned into a fish, and dove down to the bottom.

sentences.t: فَاِنْقَلَبَ الدِّيكُ حُوتًا كَبِيرًا وَنَزَلَ خَلْفَهَا وَغَابَ سَاعَةً وَإِذَا قَلْ سَمِعْنَا صُرَاخًا عَلَا وَعِيَاطًا فَاِرْتَجَفْنَا
sentences.tr: fa-inqalaba al-dīku ḥūtan kabīran wa-nazala khalfahā wa-ghāba sāʿatan wa-idhā qad samiʿnā ṣurākhan ʿalā wa-ʿiyāṭan fa-irtajafnā
sentences.l: So the rooster turned into a big fish, and went down after her, and disappeared for a while; and behold, we had already heard a rising screaming and a shrieking, and we trembled.
sentences.i: The rooster turned into a great fish and dove down after her, and vanished for a time — and behold, we had already heard a scream rise up and a shrieking, and we shook with fear.
sentences.n: قَلْ here is the same letter-substitution misprint for قَدْ as elsewhere in this scene: 'wa-idhā qad samiʿnā' ('and behold, we had already heard') is the ordinary idhā-qad construction of sudden discovery, and reads far more naturally than treating an unnamed 'he' as speaking. قَدْ is adopted here, matching the reading given to the same spelling both above at P99L04 and below at P99L19-20.

sentences.t: فَبَعْدَ ذَلِكَ طَلَعَ الْعِفْرِيتُ وَهُوَ شُعْلَةُ نَارٍ يَفْتَحُ فَمَهُ يَخْرُجُ مِنْهُ نَارٌ وَمِنْ عَيْنَيْهِ وَأَنْفِهِ نَارٌ وَدُخَانٌ وَ خَرَجَتِ الصَّبِيَّةُ وَهِيَ جَمْرَةُ نَارٍ عَظِيمَةٍ فَتَقَاتَلَا هِيَ وَإِيَّاهُ سَاعَةً حَتَّى اِنْعَقَدَتْ عَلَيْهِمَا النِّيرَانُ وَاِنْحَبَسَ الدُّخَانُ فِي الْقَصْرِ
sentences.tr: fa-baʿda dhālika ṭalaʿa al-ʿifrītu wa-huwa shuʿlatu nārin yaftaḥu famahu yakhruju minhu nārun wa-min ʿaynayhi wa-anfihi nārun wa-dukhānun wa-kharajati al-ṣabiyyatu wa-hiya jamratu nārin ʿaẕīmatin fa-taqātalā hiya wa-iyyāhu sāʿatan ḥattā inʿaqadat ʿalayhimā al-nīrānu wa-inḥabasa al-dukhānu fī al-qaṣri
sentences.l: After that the efrit rose up, he being a flame of fire, opening his mouth — fire coming out of it, and from his eyes and his nose fire and smoke — and the girl came out, she being a huge ember of fire, and the two of them, she and he, fought for a while, until the fires closed upon them both and the smoke was shut up in the palace.
sentences.i: After that the efrit rose up as a pillar of flame, opening his mouth to spit fire, fire and smoke pouring from his eyes and nose as well; and the girl came out as a huge glowing ember, and the two of them fought together for a time, until the flames closed in around them both and the smoke was trapped inside the palace.

sentences.t: فَخَفِينَا وَأَرَدْنَا أَنْ نَغْطَسَ فِي الْمَاءِ وَخِفْنَا عَلَى أَنْفُسِنَا مِنَ الْحَرِيقِ وَالْهَلَاكِ
sentences.tr: fa-khafīnā wa-aradnā an naghṭasa fī al-māʼi wa-khifnā ʿalā anfusinā min al-ḥarīqi wa-al-halāki
sentences.l: So we hid, and we wanted to dive into the water, and we feared for ourselves from the burning and the destruction.
sentences.i: We hid ourselves and wanted to plunge into the water, fearing for our own lives from the fire and ruin.
sentences.n: خَفِينَا ('we hid') and خِفْنَا ('we feared') sit side by side as a near-minimal pair, a bit of wordplay the plain narration seems to enjoy.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْمَلِكُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-maliku
sentences.l: Then the king said —
sentences.n: This sentence ends here, right at the dash before the king's own words, which open the next line.

sentences.t: لَا حَوْلَ وَلَا قُوَّةَ إِلَّا بِاللَّهِ الْعَلِيِّ الْعَظِيمِ إِنَّا لِلَّهِ وَإِنَّا إِلَيْهِ رَاجِعُونَ
sentences.tr: lā ḥawla wa-lā quwwata illā bi-Allāhi al-ʿaliyyi al-ʿaẓīmi — innā li-Allāhi wa-innā ilayhi rājiʿūna
sentences.l: There is no power and no strength except in God, the High, the Great — verily we (belong) to God, and verily to Him we return.
sentences.i: There is no strength and no power save in God, the High, the Mighty. We belong to God, and to Him we shall return.
sentences.n: This opens with two Qur'anic formulas: lā ḥawla wa-lā quwwata illā bi-Allāh (a cry of helplessness before disaster) and innā li-llāhi wa-innā ilayhi rājiʿūn (Q. 2:156, recited on hearing of death). Note that the bare انا here is read as innā ('verily we', matching the Qur'an), not anā ('I') as in the many other instances of انا later in this passage — the two are visually identical once the hamza is stripped.

sentences.t: يَا لَيْتَنَا مَا كَلَّفْنَاهَا بِذٰلِكَ فِي خَلَاصِ هٰذَا الْقِرْدِ حَتَّى أَنَّنَا أَتْعَبْنَاهَا هٰذَا التَّعَبَ الْعَظِيمَ مَعَ هٰذَا الْعِفْرِيتِ الْمَلْعُونِ الَّذِي مَا تَقْلِرُ عَلَيْهِ كُلُّ هٰذِهِ الْعَفَارِيتِ الْمَوْجُودِينَ فِي الدُّنْيَا وَيَا لَيْتَنَا مَا عَرَفْنَا هٰذَا الْقِرْدَ لَا بَارَكَ اللَّهُ فِيهِ وَلَا فِي سَاعَتِهِ
sentences.tr: yā laytanā mā kallafnāhā bi-dhālika fī khalāṣi hādhā al-qirdi ḥattā annanā atʿabnāhā hādhā al-taʿaba al-ʿaẒīma maʿa hādhā al-ʿifrīti al-malʿūni alladhī mā taqliru ʿalayhi kullu hādhihi al-ʿafārīti al-mawjūdīna fī al-dunyā — wa-yā laytanā mā ʿarafnā hādhā al-qirda; lā bāraka Allāhu fīhi wa-lā fī sāʿatihi.
sentences.l: Oh, would that we had not charged her with that, in the freeing of this monkey, so that we did tire her — this great tiring — with this cursed efrit, whom all these efrits existing in the world cannot overpower! And would that we had not known this monkey — may God not bless him, nor his hour!
sentences.i: Would that we had never asked her to free this monkey at all — that we wore her out so terribly against this accursed efrit, whom no efrit alive in the world could master! And would that we had never set eyes on this monkey — God bless him not, nor the hour he ever came to us!
sentences.n: هٰذَا, هٰذِهِ, ذٰلِكَ and كَذٰلِكَ are defective spellings (missing the internal long ā), marked here with the dagger alif; this is standard even in fully classical orthography, not a Middle Arabic quirk. تقلر is almost certainly a dāl/lām misprint for تَقْدِرُ 'is able' (compare قَلْ for قَدْ a few lines below, and القصر قل انقلب elsewhere in this tale) — vocalized here as printed, read 'cannot overpower'. Note that the speaker refers to the enchanted young man throughout as 'this monkey' in the third person, even while cursing him — the young man is in fact narrating his own past self.

sentences.t: قَصَدْنَا أَنْ نَعْمَلَ مَعَهُ جَمِيلًا لِوَجْهِ اللَّهِ تَعَالَى وَنُخَلِّصَهُ مِنَ السِّحْرِ فَاُبْتُلِينَا بِتَعَبِ الْقَلْبِ وَأَنَا يَا سِتِّي مَرْبُوطُ اللِّسَانِ لَمْ أَقْدِرْ أَنْكَلِمَ مَعَهُ بِشَيْءٍ
sentences.tr: qaṣadnā an naʿmala maʿahu jamīlan li-wajhi Allāhi taʿālā wa-nukhalliṣahu mina al-siḥri fa-ubtulīnā bi-taʿabi al-qalbi — wa-anā, yā sittī, marbūṭu al-lisāni, lam aqdir ankalima maʿahu bi-shayʾin.
sentences.l: We intended to do him a good deed, for the sake of God most high, and to free him from the sorcery — so we were afflicted with heartache. And I, my lady, [was] bound of tongue: I was not able to converse with him about anything.
sentences.i: We only meant to do him a kindness for God's sake, and free him from the spell — and for it we were struck with heartache. And I, my lady, was tongue-tied: I could not say a word to him.
sentences.n: مربوط اللسان, literally 'bound of tongue', means rendered speechless (he was still in the ape's shape and could not talk). أنكلم is read as a Middle Arabic Form VII (from k-l-m) standing in for the classical أَتَكَلَّمَ 'I converse', after an elided أن following أقدر. سِتِّي, 'my lady', is colloquial (from ست, itself colloquial for سيدة).

sentences.t: ثُمَّ مَا شَعَرْنَا إِلَّا وَالْعِفْرِيتُ قَلْ صَرَخَ مِنْ تَحْتِ النِّيرَانِ وَصَارَ عِنْدَنَا فِي الْإِيوَانِ وَنَفَخَ فِي وُجُوهِنَا بِالنَّارِ فَلَحِقَتْهُ الصَّبِيَّةُ وَنَفَخَتْ فِي وَجْهِهِ فَأَصَابَنَا الشَّرَارُ مِنْهَا وَ مِنْهُ
sentences.tr: thumma mā shaʿarnā illā wa-al-ʿifrītu qal ṣarakha min taḥti al-nīrāni wa-ṣāra ʿindanā fī al-īwāni wa-nafakha fī wujūhinā bi-al-nāri — fa-laḥiqathu al-ṣabiyyatu wa-nafakhat fī wajhihi, fa-aṣābanā al-sharāru minhā wa-minhu.
sentences.l: Then we did not notice, except that the efrit had already shrieked from beneath the fires and had come to be with us in the hall, and blew fire into our faces. So the girl matched him and blew into his face — and the sparks struck us, from her and from him.
sentences.i: Then, before we knew it, the efrit let out a shriek from under the flames and was suddenly standing among us in the hall, blasting fire into our faces. At once the girl met him and blew fire back into his — and sparks from them both came raining down on us.
sentences.n: 'ما شعرنا إلا و...' is a stock idiom of sudden surprise: 'before we knew it...'. قل here stands for قَدْ ('already'), a dāl/lām misprint (compare تقلر above, and القصر قل انقلب elsewhere in this tale). الإيوان ('the hall') is a Persian loanword for a vaulted audience-hall; its hamza is supplied here since the source prints it bare.

sentences.t: فَأَمَّا شَرَارُهَا فَلَمْ يُؤْذِنَا وَأَمَّا شَرَارُهُ فَلَحِقَتِي فِي عَيْنِي شَرَارَةٌ فَأَمْسَكْتُهَا وَأَنَا فِي صُورَةِ الْقِرْدِ
sentences.tr: fa-ammā sharāruhā fa-lam yuʾdhinā, wa-ammā sharāruhu fa-laḥiqatī fī ʿaynī sharāratun fa-amsaktuhā, wa-anā fī ṣūrati al-qirdi.
sentences.l: As for her sparks, they did not harm us; but as for his sparks — there struck [me], in my eye, a spark, and I caught it, I being in the monkey's shape.
sentences.i: Her sparks did us no harm; but his — one struck me in the eye, and I caught it, still in my monkey's form.
sentences.n: فلحقتي is printed without the expected نـ of the object suffix (-نـي, 'me'); read as لَحِقَتْنِي, 'it struck me' — likely a scribal contraction. This clause is the enchanted young man's own aside, singling out his individual experience (still monkey-shaped) from the surrounding 'we' of the king's household — the injury to this eye is why, once restored to human shape, he will be one-eyed for the rest of his life as a qalandar.

sentences.t: وَلَحِقَ الْمَلِكَ شَرَارَةٌ مِنْهُ فِي وَجْهِهِ أَحْرَفَتْ نِصْفَ وَجْهِهِ وَذَقَنَهُ وَحَنَكَهُ التَّحْنَانِيَّ وَأَوْنَعَتْ صَفَّ أَسْنَاهُ التَّحْنَانِيَّةَ
sentences.tr: wa-laḥiqa al-malika sharāratun minhu fī wajhihi, aḥrafat niṣfa wajhihi wa-dhaqanahu wa-ḥanakahu al-taḥnāniyya, wa-awnaʿat ṣaffa asnāhu al-taḥnāniyyata.
sentences.l: And there struck the king a spark from him, in his face — [it] burned half his face, his chin, and his lower jaw; and it damaged the row of his lower teeth.
sentences.i: A spark from him also caught the king full in the face, burning half his face, his chin, and his lower jaw, and damaging his lower teeth as well.
sentences.n: أحرفت (with ف) is almost certainly a misprint for أَحْرَقَتْ 'burned' (qāf/fāʾ confusion) — vocalized as printed. التحناني/التحنانية most likely stand for التحتاني/التحتانية, 'lower' (a tāʾ/nūn mix-up, or a dialectal variant), read that way. أونعت is obscure — perhaps a misprint for أَوْجَعَتْ 'pained' or أَوْقَعَتْ 'struck'; rendered here by sense. أسناه drops the نـ of أَسْنَانَهُ 'his teeth', a colloquial contraction of the broken plural.

sentences.t: وَقَعَتْ شَرَارَةٌ فِي صَدْرِ الطَّوَاشِي فَاحْتَرَقَ وَمَاتَ مِنْ وَقْتِهِ وَسَاعَتِهِ فَأَيْقَنَّا بِالْهَلَاكِ وَأَيِسْنَا مِنَ الْحَيَوةِ
sentences.tr: waqaʿat sharāratun fī ṣadri al-ṭawāshī, fa-iḥtaraqa wa-māta min waqtihi wa-sāʿatihi — fa-ayqannā bi-al-halāki wa-ayisnā mina al-ḥayāti.
sentences.l: A spark fell on the chest of the chamberlain, so he burned and died on the spot, that very moment — so we became certain of destruction, and we despaired of life.
sentences.i: A spark fell on the chamberlain's chest, and he burned to death instantly. We were sure we were doomed, and gave up hope of living.
sentences.n: الحيوة is the older spelling of الحياة, 'life', with wāw standing in for the long ā (compare صلوة for الصلاة elsewhere in this convention); kept as printed, read ḥayāh.

sentences.t: فَبَيْنَمَا نَحْنُ كَذٰلِكَ وَ إِذَا بِقَائِلٍ يَقُولُ اللَّهُ أَكْبَرُ اللَّهُ أَكْبَرُ فَتْحٌ وَنَصْرٌ وَخَذْلٌ مَنْ كَفَرَ بِدِينِ مُحَمَّدٍ الْقَمَرُ وَإِذَا بِهَا بِبِنْتِ الْمَلِكِ قَدْ أَحْرَقَتْ الْعِفْرِيتَ وَ إِذَا بِهِ قَدْ صَارَ كَوْمَ رَمَادٍ
sentences.tr: fa-baynamā naḥnu ka-dhālika wa-idhā bi-qāʾilin yaqūlu: Allāhu akbaru, Allāhu akbaru, fatḥun wa-naṣrun wa-khadhlun man kafara bi-dīni Muḥammadin! Al-qamaru — wa-idhā bihā bi-binti al-maliki qad aḥraqati al-ʿifrīta, wa-idhā bihi qad ṣāra kawma ramādin.
sentences.l: And while we were thus, behold, there was a speaker saying: 'God is greatest, God is greatest — a victory, and a triumph, and a rout for whoever disbelieves in the religion of Muhammad!' The moon! — and behold her, the king's daughter, had burned the efrit; and behold him, he had become a heap of ashes.
sentences.i: And while we stood like this, a voice suddenly rang out: 'God is greatest! God is greatest! Victory, triumph, and ruin for whoever denies the faith of Muhammad!' The moon of a girl! — and there she was, the king's daughter, having burnt the efrit to nothing; and there he was, turned to a heap of ashes.
sentences.n: وَإِذَا بِهَا بِبِنْتِ الْمَلِكِ ... وَإِذَا بِهِ: the بِـ after إِذَا of surprise marks what suddenly appears rather than meaning 'with' — 'and behold, there she was, the king's daughter, having burnt the efrit; and there he was, become a heap of ashes' — as at P98L07-09 above and again below at P102L16. القمر ('the moon') sits oddly between the victory-cry and the following clause; it may be an admiring exclamation about the princess ('the moon [of a girl]!'), which is the reading given here, or the text may simply be corrupt at this point — no fully certain reading is possible. خذل ('a routing') is vocalized as a verbal noun parallel to فتح and نصر.

sentences.t: وَجَاءَتْ الصَّبِيَّةُ إِلَيْنَا وَقَالَتْ أَلْحِقُونِي بِطَاسَةِ مَاءٍ فَجَاوَا بِهَا إِلَيْهَا فَتَكَلَّمَتْ عَلَيْهَا بِكَلَامٍ لَا نَفْهَمُهُ ثُمَّ طَرَشَتْنِي بِالْمَاءِ وَقَالَتْ اُخْلُصْ بِحَقِّ الْحَقِّ وَبِحَقِّ اِسْمِ اللَّهِ الْأَعْظَمِ إِلَى صُورَتِكَ الْأُولَى
sentences.tr: wa-jāʾat al-ṣabiyyatu ilaynā wa-qālat: 'alḥiqūnī bi-ṭāsati māʾin.' Fa-jāwā bihā ilayhā, fa-takallamat ʿalayhā bi-kalāmin lā nafhamuhu, thumma ṭarashatnī bi-al-māʾi wa-qālat: 'ukhluṣ, bi-ḥaqqi al-ḥaqqi wa-bi-ḥaqqi ismi Allāhi al-aʿẓami, ilā ṣūratika al-ūlā!'
sentences.l: And the girl came to us and said: 'Bring me quickly a bowl of water.' So they brought it to her, and she spoke over it words we did not understand; then she sprinkled me with the water and said: 'Be freed — by the truth of the Truth, and by the truth of the greatest name of God — to your first shape!'
sentences.i: The girl came to us and said, 'Bring me a bowl of water, quickly!' They brought it to her; she spoke some words over it that we could not make out, then flicked the water at me and said: 'Be released — by the truth of the Truth, and by the greatest name of God — back into your first shape!'
sentences.n: فجاوا (for فَجَاؤُوا, 'so they brought') is printed without any hamza letter at all — a colloquial contraction, not the usual bare-alif-for-hamza pattern seen elsewhere. اخلص is read as the plain imperative اُخْلُصْ, 'be freed/released' (Form I, hamzat al-waṣl).

sentences.t: قَالَ فَانْتَفَضْتُ فَإِذَا أَنَا بَشَرٌ كَمَا كُنْتُ وَلٰكِنْ رَاحَتْ عَيْنِي
sentences.tr: Qāla: fa-intafaḍtu, fa-idhā anā basharun kamā kuntu, wa-lākin rāḥat ʿaynī.
sentences.l: He said: 'So I shook, and there I was, a human, as I had been — but my eye was gone.'
sentences.i: He said: 'I gave a shudder, and found myself human again, just as I had been — except that I had lost my eye.'
sentences.n: قال briefly marks a return to third-person narration introducing the enchanted young man's own words. This is the moment the tale's teller — a one-eyed wandering qalandar — loses the eye that will mark him for the rest of his life.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ الصَّبِيَّةُ النَّارُ النَّارُ يَا وَالِدِي مَا بَقِيتُ أَعِيشُ وَمَا أَنَا مُعَوَّدَةٌ بِقِتَالِ الْجِنِّ وَ لَوْ كَانَ مِنَ الْإِنْسِ تَقْتُلُهُ مِنْ زَمَانٍ
sentences.tr: Fa-qālat al-ṣabiyyatu: 'al-nāru, al-nāru! Yā wālidī, mā baqītu aʿīshu, wa-mā anā muʿawwadatun bi-qitāli al-jinni, wa-law kāna mina al-insi taqtuluhu min zamānin —
sentences.l: Then the girl said: 'The fire! The fire! O my father, I shall not go on living — I am not accustomed to fighting jinn, and had he been of mankind, [one] would have killed him long ago —'
sentences.i: The girl cried out: 'The fire! The fire! Father, I will not live — I am not used to fighting jinn, and if he had been human, he'd have been dead long since —'
sentences.n: تقتله is ambiguous in form between 'you (m.) kill him' and 'she kills him' (identical spelling); taken here as a generic 'one', i.e. 'he would have been killed easily'.

sentences.t: وَمَا تَعِبْتُ إِلَّا وَقْتَ فَرْطِ الرُّمَّانَةِ وَ لَقْطِ حَبِّهَا وَنَسِيتُ الْحَبَّةَ الَّتِي فِيهَا رُوحُ الْجِنِّيِّ فَلَوْ لَقَطْتُهَا لَمَاتَ مِنْ سَاعَتِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-mā taʿibtu illā waqta farṭi al-rummānati wa-laqṭi ḥabbihā, wa-nasītu al-ḥabbata allatī fīhā rūḥu al-jinniyyi — fa-law laqaṭtuhā la-māta min sāʿatihi —
sentences.l: and I only grew weary at the moment of the pomegranate's spilling and the gathering of its seeds, and I forgot the seed in which was the jinni's life — for had I picked it up, he would have died on the spot —
sentences.i: the only moment I faltered was when the pomegranate burst and its seeds scattered — I forgot the one seed that held the jinni's life. Had I caught it, he would have died then and there —
sentences.n: This is the crux of her account: the shape-shifting duel ends with the efrit becoming a pomegranate that bursts into scattered seeds, one of which held his life unless caught — a version of the widespread 'external soul' motif. Her single lapse, missing that seed, let him revive and drag the fight into fire.

sentences.t: وَلٰكِنْ مَا عَلِمْتُ بِالْقَضَا وَالْقَدَرِ فَإِذَا هُوَ قَدْ أَتَى وَجَرَى لِي مَعَهُ حَرْبٌ شَدِيدٌ تَحْتَ الْأَرْضِ وَفِي الْهَوَاءِ وَالْمَاءِ وَكُلَّمَا أَفْتَحُ عَلَيْهِ بَابًا يَفْتَحُ عَلَيَّ بَابًا إِلَى أَنْ فَتَحَ عَلَيَّ بَابُ النَّارِ وَقَلِيلٌ مَنْ يَفْتَحُ عَلَيْهِ بَابُ النَّارِ وَهُوَ يَنْجُو مِنْهُ
sentences.tr: wa-lākin mā ʿalimtu bi-al-qaḏā wa-al-qadari, fa-idhā huwa qad atā, wa-jarā lī maʿahu ḥarbun shadīdun taḥta al-arḍi wa-fī al-hawāʾi wa-al-māʾi, wa-kullamā aftaḥu ʿalayhi bāban yaftaḥu ʿalayya bāban, ilā an fataḥa ʿalayya bābu al-nāri — wa-qalīlun man yaftaḥu ʿalayhi bābu al-nāri wa-huwa yanjū minhu —
sentences.l: but I did not reckon with fate and destiny — and behold, he had come, and there was between him and me a fierce war, beneath the earth, and in the air, and in the water; and every time I opened against him a door, he opened against me a door — until the door of fire opened against me. And few are they against whom the door of fire opens, and they escape it —
sentences.i: but I hadn't reckoned with fate — and there he was, come back, and a fierce war broke out between us, under the earth, in the air, and in the water. Every door I opened against him, he opened one against me — until the door of fire opened against me. Few indeed are those the fire-door opens against who escape it —
sentences.n: القضا is a defective spelling of القضاء ('the decree') printed without the final hamza, kept as printed. The duel runs through the classic sequence earth, air, water, then fire; note how the last door — بَابُ النَّارِ — becomes the grammatical subject that itself 'opens', rather than an object she or the efrit opens, as if the fire took on a life of its own.

sentences.t: وَإِنَّمَا سَاعَدَنِي عَلَيْهِ الْقَدَرُ حَتَّى حَرَقْتُهُ قَبْلِي وَكُنْتُ أَعْهَدُ مِنْهُ بِدِينِ الْإِسْلَامِ وَأَمَّا أَنَا مَيِّتَةٌ فَخَلِيفَتِي اللَّهُ عَلَيْكُمْ
sentences.tr: wa-innamā sāʿadanī ʿalayhi al-qadaru ḥattā ḥaraqtuhu qablī, wa-kuntu aʿhadu minhu bi-dīni al-islāmi — wa-ammā anā mayyitatun fa-khalīfatī Allāhu ʿalaykum.'
sentences.l: It was only fate that helped me against him, so that I burned him before myself; and I used to know of him [that he was] of the religion of Islam. And as for me, I am dying — so my successor over you [is] God.'
sentences.i: It was fate alone that let me get the better of him, so that I burned him before he could finish me. I had always known him to hold to the faith of Islam. As for me, I am dying — so let God take my place watching over you.'
sentences.n: فخليفتي الله عليكم is a set dying-formula, naming God as guardian/successor over those left behind.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَنَّهَا اِسْتَغَاثَتْ وَلَمْ تَزَلْ تَسْتَغِيثُ مِنَ النَّارِ فَإِذَا شَرَارٌ أَسْوَدُ قَدْ طَلَعَ إِلَى صَدْرِهَا وَطَلَعَ إِلَى وَجْهِهَا فَلَمَّا وَصَلَ إِلَى وَجْهِهَا بَكَتْ وَقَالَتْ أَشْهَدُ أَنْ لَا إِلٰهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ وَأَنَّ مُحَمَّدًا رَسُولُ اللَّهِ
sentences.tr: Thumma annahā istaghāthat wa-lam tazal tastaghīthu mina al-nāri, fa-idhā sharārun aswadu qad ṭalaʿa ilā ṣadrihā wa-ṭalaʿa ilā wajhihā; fa-lammā waṣala ilā wajhihā, bakat wa-qālat: 'ashhadu an lā ilāha illā Allāhu wa-anna Muḥammadan rasūlu Allāhi.'
sentences.l: Then she cried out for help, and did not cease crying out for help from the fire — and behold, a black spark had risen to her chest, and risen to her face; and when it reached her face, she wept and said: 'I testify that there is no god but God, and that Muhammad is the messenger of God.'
sentences.i: Then she cried out against the fire, and kept crying out — until a black spark rose to her chest, then to her face; and as it reached her face, she wept and said: 'I bear witness that there is no god but God, and that Muhammad is His messenger.'
sentences.n: Her last words are the shahāda, the Muslim declaration of faith, spoken as the fire consumes her.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ نَظَرْنَا إِلَيْهَا وَإِذَا بِهَا كَوْمُ رَمَادٍ إِلَى جَانِبِ كَوْمِ الْعِفْرِيتِ
sentences.tr: Thumma naẓarnā ilayhā, wa-idhā bihā kawmu ramādin ilā jānibi kawmi al-ʿifrīti.
sentences.l: Then we looked at her, and behold, she [was] a heap of ashes, beside the heap of the efrit.
sentences.i: Then we looked at her — and there she was, a heap of ashes, lying beside the efrit's own heap of ashes.

sentences.t: فَحَزِنَّا عَلَيْهَا وَتَمَنَّيْتُ لَوْ كُنْتُ مَكَانَهَا وَلَا أَرَى ذٰلِكَ الْوَجْهَ الْمَلِيحَ الَّذِي يَعْمَلُ فِي هٰذَا الْخَيْرِ يَصِيرُ رَمَادًا لٰكِنْ حُكْمُ اللَّهِ لَا يُرَدُّ
sentences.tr: fa-ḥazinnā ʿalayhā wa-tamannaytu law kuntu makānahā wa-lā arā dhālika al-wajha al-malīḥa alladhī yaʿmalu fī hādhā al-khayri yaṣīru ramādan lākin ḥukmu allāhi lā yuraddu
sentences.l: So we grieved for her, and I wished that I were in her place, and would not see that handsome face — which does such good — become ashes; but the decree of God is not turned back.
sentences.i: So we grieved for her, and I wished I had been in her place, never to see that lovely face, so full of goodness, turn to ashes; but the decree of God cannot be turned back.
sentences.n: The edition prints bare alif for hamza almost everywhere (أرى → ارى); we mark it with a combining hamza on the alif rather than the precomposed أ, since the archive's own bare spelling must remain recoverable letter-for-letter. 'الخير' here likely means her goodness of character rather than material wealth.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَى الْمَلِكُ ابْنَتَهُ صَارَتْ كَوْمَ رَمَادٍ نَتَفَ بَقِيَّةَ لِحْيَتِهِ وَلَطَمَ عَلَى وَجْهِهِ وَشَقَّ أَثْوَابَهُ وَفَعَلَتْ كَمَا فَعَلَ وَبَكَيْنَا عَلَيْهَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾā al-maliku ibnatahu ṣārat kawma ramādin nataf baqiyyata liḥyatihi wa-laṭama ʿalā wajhihi wa-shaqqa athwābahu wa-faʿalat kamā faʿala wa-bakaynā ʿalayhā
sentences.l: So when the king saw [that] his daughter had become a heap of ashes, he tore out what remained of his beard, and struck his face, and rent his garments; and she did as he did; and we wept over her.
sentences.i: When the king saw that his daughter had turned into a heap of ashes, he tore out what was left of his beard, struck his own face, and rent his garments; the queen did as he did, and we wept over her.
sentences.n: 'وفعلت كما فعل' leaves the second actor unnamed (almost certainly the queen); the mirrored grief-gestures of king and queen form a small parallel pair typical of the Nights' mourning scenes.

sentences.t: فَجَاءُوا الْحُجَّابُ وَأَرْبَابُ الدَّوْلَةِ فَوَجَدُوا السُّلْطَانَ فِي حَالَةِ الْعَدَمِ وَكَوْمَيْنِ رَمَادًا فَتَعَجَّبُوا وَ دَارُوا حَوْلَ الْمَلِكِ سَاعَةً
sentences.tr: fa-jāʾū al-ḥujjābu wa-arbābu al-dawlati fa-wajadū al-sulṭāna fī ḥālati al-ʿadami wa-kawmayni ramādan fa-taʿajjabū wa-dārū ḥawla al-maliki sāʿatan
sentences.l: Then the chamberlains and the lords of the state came, and found the sultan in a state of senselessness, and two heaps of ashes; and they were astonished, and circled around the king for a while.
sentences.i: Then the chamberlains and the great officers of state came in, and found the sultan bereft of his senses, with two heaps of ashes before him; they marveled, and circled round the king for a time.
sentences.n: 'جاءوا' already carries a precomposed hamza (ء) in the edition's own spelling, so — unlike 'ارى' or 'ارباب' — it is kept precomposed rather than converted to the combining-hamza notation.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا أَفَاقَ أَخْبَرَهُمْ بِمَا جَرَى لِابْنَتِهِ مَعَ الْعِفْرِيتِ فَعَظُمَتْ مُصِيبَتُهُمْ وَصَرَخَ النِّسَاءُ وَالْجَوَارِي وَأَقَامُوا الْعَزَاءَ سَبْعَةَ أَيَّامٍ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā afāqa akhbarahum bimā jarā li-ibnatihi maʿa al-ʿifrīti fa-ʿaẕumat muṣībatuhum wa-ṣarakha al-nisāʾu wa-al-jawārī wa-aqāmū al-ʿazāʾa sabʿata ayyāmin
sentences.l: So when he recovered, he told them what had happened to his daughter with the efrit; so their calamity grew great, and the women and slave-girls cried out, and they held mourning seven days.
sentences.i: When he came to himself, he told them what had befallen his daughter at the efrit's hands; their grief grew heavier still, the women and slave-girls shrieked aloud, and mourning was kept for seven days.
sentences.n: 'وصرخ' is masculine though its subject 'النساء والجواري' is feminine plural — a Middle Arabic feature (verb not matching the gender of a following subject) rather than an error; we vocalize it as printed and flag it here as the first clear instance in this night's text.

sentences.t: وَقَامَ الْمَلِكُ وَأَمَرَ أَنْ يَبْنِيَ عَلَى رَمَادِ ابْنَتِهِ قُبَّةً عَظِيمَةً وَ أَوْقَدُوا فِيهَا الشُّمُوعَ وَالْقَنَادِيلَ وَأَمَّا رَمَادُ الْعِفْرِيتِ فَإِنَّهُمْ ذَرَوْهُ فِي الْهَوَاءِ إِلَى لَعْنَةِ اللَّهِ
sentences.tr: wa-qāma al-maliku wa-amara an yabniya ʿalā ramādi ibnatihi qubbatan ʿaẕīmatan wa-awqadū fīhā al-shumūʿa wa-al-qanādīla wa-ammā ramādu al-ʿifrīti fa-innahum dharawhu fī al-hawāʾi ilā laʿnati allāhi
sentences.l: And the king arose, and ordered that [one] build over his daughter's ashes a great dome; and they lit therein the candles and the lamps. And as for the efrit's ashes, they scattered them into the air, unto the curse of God.
sentences.i: The king then arose and ordered a great dome raised over his daughter's ashes, with candles and lamps kept burning inside it. As for the efrit's ashes, they scattered them upon the wind, to the curse of God.
sentences.n: The edition spells this verb 'يبني' with a dotted yā, not alif maqṣūra; taken literally that gives active 'yabniya' ('that [one] build a dome', قبة as its object) rather than the passive 'yubnā' one might expect — we keep the letter as printed rather than silently correcting it to the passive spelling. 'إلى لعنة الله' is a formulaic malediction, 'to God's curse [be they given]'.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ مَرِضَ السُّلْطَانُ مَرَضًا أَشْرَفَ مِنْهُ عَلَى الْمَوْتِ وَمُدَّةُ مَرَضِهِ شَهْرٌ وَأَتَتْ إِلَيْهِ الْعَافِيَةُ وَنَبَتَتْ لِحْيَتُهُ فَطَلَبَنِي
sentences.tr: thumma mariḍa al-sulṭānu maraḍan ashrafa minhu ʿalā al-mawti wa-muddatu maraḍihi shahrun wa-atat ilayhi al-ʿāfiyatu wa-nabatat liḥyatuhu fa-ṭalabanī
sentences.l: Then the sultan fell ill with an illness by which he came to the brink of death; and the term of his illness was a month; then health came to him, and his beard grew back; and he sent for me.
sentences.i: Then the sultan fell so gravely ill that he came near to death; his illness lasted a month, until health returned to him and his beard grew back — and he sent for me.
sentences.n: 'أشرف على الموت' is the idiom 'to be at the very brink of death'.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ لِي يَا فَتَى قَدْ قَضَيْنَا زَمَانَنَا فِي أَهْنَى عَيْشٍ آمِنِينَ مِنْ نَوَائِبِ الزَّمَانِ حَتَّى أَقْبَلْتَ عَلَيْنَا يَا لَيْتَنَا مَا كُنَّا رَأَيْنَاكَ وَلَا رَأَيْنَا يَوْمَ طَلْعَتَكَ الْقَبِيحَةَ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla lī yā fatā qad qaḍaynā zamānanā fī ahnā ʿayshin āminīna min nawāʾibi al-zamāni ḥattā aqbalta ʿalaynā yā laytanā mā kunnā raʾaynāka wa-lā raʾaynā yawma ṭalʿataka al-qabīḥata
sentences.l: And he said to me, 'O young man, we had spent our time in the most pleasant living, safe from the calamities of fate, until you came upon us. Would that we had not seen you, nor seen the day of your ugly arrival!'
sentences.i: He said to me, 'O young man, we had passed our days in the sweetest of lives, safe from the blows of fortune, until you descended upon us. Would that we had never set eyes on you, nor lived to see the day of your ill-omened coming!'
sentences.n: 'آمنين' and 'نوائب' are both already spelled with a precomposed hamza-bearing letter (آ, ئ) in the edition, unlike 'أهنى'/'أقبلت'/etc., and are kept exactly as given. 'طلعتك القبيحة', literally 'your ugly rising/appearance', is an idiom of ill omen about the young man's arrival, not a remark on his looks.

sentences.t: فَإِحْنَا صِرْنَا فِي حَالَةِ الْعَدَمِ بِسَبَبِكَ الْأَوَّلُ عَدِمْتُ ابْنَتِي الَّتِي كَانَتْ تُسَاوِي مِائَةَ رَجُلٍ وَالثَّانِي جَرَى لِي مِنَ الْحَرِيقِ مَا جَرَى وَ عَدِمْتُ أَضْرَاسِي وَمَاتَ خَادِمِي
sentences.tr: fa-iḥnā ṣirnā fī ḥālati al-ʿadami bi-sababika al-awwalu ʿadimtu ibnatī allatī kānat tusāwī miʾata rajulin wa-al-thānī jarā lī mina al-ḥarīqi mā jarā wa-ʿadimtu aḍrāsī wa-māta khādimī
sentences.l: So we fell into a state of ruin because of you: the first — I lost my daughter, who was worth a hundred men; and the second — there happened to me from the fire what happened, and I lost my molars, and my servant died.
sentences.i: Thus we were brought to ruin on your account: first, I lost my daughter, who was worth a hundred men; second, the fire wrought upon me what it wrought, and I lost my teeth, and my servant died.
sentences.n: 'إحنا' (for classical 'نحن', 'we') is colloquial/dialectal, kept as a Middle Arabic feature rather than corrected. 'الأول... والثاني' is used adverbially, 'firstly... secondly'.

sentences.t: وَقَبْلَ ذٰلِكَ وَبَعْدَهُ مَا رَأَيْنَا مِنْكَ شَيْئًا بَلِ الْكُلُّ مِنَ اللَّهِ عَلَيْكَ وَعَلَيْنَا وَالْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ وَأَنْتَ الَّذِي خَلَّصَتْكَ ابْنَتِي وَأَهْلَكَتْ نَفْسَهَا
sentences.tr: wa-qabla dhālika wa-baʿdahu mā raʾaynā minka shayʾan bali al-kullu mina allāhi ʿalayka wa-ʿalaynā wa-al-ḥamdu lillāhi wa-anta alladhī khallaṣatka ibnatī wa-ahlakat nafsahā
sentences.l: And before that and after it, we saw nothing from you; rather, it is all from God, upon you and upon us; and the praise is God's. And you are the one whom my daughter saved, destroying herself.
sentences.i: Both before that and after, we saw no wrong in you; all of it is from God, upon you as upon us — praise be to God. It was my daughter who saved you, and in doing so destroyed herself.
sentences.n: The king here explicitly absolves the young man of fault even while blaming him as the occasion of the disaster — the note that follows this speech turns on that very distinction.

sentences.t: فَاخْرُجْ يَا وَلَدِي مِنْ بَلَدِي وَكَفَى مَا جَرَى بِسَبَبِكَ وَكُلُّ ذٰلِكَ مُقَدَّرٌ عَلَيْنَا وَعَلَيْكَ فَاخْرُجْ بِسَلَامٍ وَإِنْ عُدْتَ رَأَيْتُكَ قَتَلْتُكَ
sentences.tr: fa-ukhruj yā waladī min baladī wa-kafā mā jarā bi-sababika wa-kullu dhālika muqaddarun ʿalaynā wa-ʿalayka fa-ukhruj bi-salāmin wa-in ʿudta raʾaytuka qataltuka
sentences.l: So go out, my son, from my land, and let what happened because of you suffice; and all of that is decreed upon us and upon you. So go out in peace; and if you return, I shall see you, [and] I shall kill you.
sentences.i: So leave my land, my son; let what has happened on your account be enough. All of it was decreed upon us as upon you. Go now in peace — but if you return, the moment I see you, I will kill you.
sentences.n: 'رأيتك قتلتك' uses the plain perfect for a future conditional result ('if you return, I see-you [and] kill-you' = 'I will see and kill you') — a normal Classical idiom for a conditional apodosis, rendered here with English future tense.

sentences.t: وَصَرَخَ عَلَيَّ فَخَرَجْتُ يَا سَيِّدِي مِنْ عِنْدِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-ṣarakha ʿalayya fa-kharajtu yā sayyidī min ʿindihi
sentences.l: And he cried out at me, so I went out, O my lord, from his presence.
sentences.i: He cried out at me, and so, my lord, I left his presence.
sentences.n: The narrating voice shifts back here from the king's direct speech to the young man himself, addressing 'يا سيدي' — the frame audience of this tale.

sentences.t: وَ مَا أُصَدِّقُ بِالنَّجَاةِ وَلَا أَدْرِي أَيْنَ أَتَوَجَّهُ وَخَطَرَ عَلَى قَلْبِي مَا جَرَى لِي وَكَيْفَ يُخَلُّونِي فِي الطَّرِيقِ وَسَلَامَتِي مِنْهُمْ
sentences.tr: wa-mā uṣaddiqu bi-al-najāti wa-lā adrī ayna atawajjahu wa-khaṭara ʿalā qalbī mā jarā lī wa-kayfa yukhallūnī fī al-ṭarīqi wa-salāmatī minhum
sentences.l: And I did not believe in [my] deliverance, nor did I know where I should turn; and there crossed my heart what had happened to me, and how they would leave me on the road, and my safety from them.
sentences.i: I could scarcely believe I had escaped, nor did I know which way to turn; all that had befallen me passed again through my mind, and I wondered how I should fare on the road, and whether I was truly safe from them.
sentences.n: 'يخلوني' is read as a colloquially reduced 'يُخَلُّونِي' ('will they leave/spare me'), with the double nūn of the plural-verb-plus-suffix simplified to one — a Middle Arabic feature. The antecedent of 'them' (منهم) is left genuinely unclear: it may look back generally to the dangers of the road, or to those he had just fled; we do not resolve it beyond what the text gives.

sentences.t: وَمَشَيْتُ شَهْرًا وَ دَخَلْتُ فِي الْمَدِينَةِ غَرِيبًا وَاجْتِمَاعِي بِالْخَيَّاطِ وَاجْتِمَاعِي بِالصَّبِيَّةِ تَحْتَ الْأَرْضِ وَخَلَاصِي مِنَ الْعِفْرِيتِ بَعْدَ أَنْ كَانَ عَازِمًا عَلَى قَتْلِي وَمَا عَبَرَ قَلْبِي مِنَ الْمُبْتَدَا وَالْمُنْتَهَى فَحَمِدْتُ اللَّهَ وَقُلْتُ بِعَيْنِي وَلَا
sentences.tr: wa-mashaytu shahran wa-dakhaltu fī al-madīnati gharīban wa-ijtimāʿī bi-al-khayyāṭi wa-ijtimāʿī bi-al-ṣabiyyati taḥta al-arḍi wa-khalāṣī mina al-ʿifrīti baʿda an kāna ʿāziman ʿalā qatlī wa-mā ʿabara qalbī mina al-mubtadā wa-al-muntahā fa-ḥamidtu allāha wa-qultu bi-ʿaynī wa-lā
sentences.l: And I journeyed a month, and entered into the city as a stranger; and [there was] my meeting with the tailor, and my meeting with the girl under the ground, and my deliverance from the efrit — after he had been resolved upon killing me; and there passed through my heart [all] from the beginning to the end; so I praised God, and I said, 'With my eye — and not—'
sentences.i: So I journeyed on for a month, and came into the city a stranger; there was my meeting with the tailor again, and my meeting with the girl from under the ground, and my deliverance from the efrit, who had been bent on killing me. All of it, from first to last, passed once more through my heart; and I gave thanks to God, and said, 'With my eye — but not—'
sentences.n: The archived text breaks off after 'ولا'; the following night completes the phrase as 'بعيني ولا بروحي' ('with my eye, but not with my soul'), i.e. his thanks was outward and formal, not heartfelt — but that word itself falls outside tonight's text and is not supplied in the Arabic here. 'المبتدا' is spelled without the expected hamza (classically 'مبتدأ'), plausibly leveled to rhyme with 'المنتهى' (mubtadā / muntahā), a small sajʿ pairing; kept as printed rather than corrected. 'تحت الارض' ('under the ground') and the tailor look back to earlier events of this same tale, narrated in an earlier night.

sentences.t: بِرُوحِي وَدَخَلْتُ الْحَمَّامَ قَبْلَ أَنْ أَخْرُجَ مِنَ الْبَلِيَّةِ وَحَلَقْتُ ذَقْنِي وَلَبِسْتُ مِسْحًا أَسْوَدَ وَحَطَّيْتُ عَلَى رَأْسِي بَا سِيدِي وَفِي كُلِّ يَوْمٍ أَبْكِي وَأَفْتَكِرُ الْمَصَائِبَ الَّتِي جَرَتْ عَلَيَّ وَقَلْعَ عَيْنِي وَكُلَّ مَا أَفْتَكِرُ جَرَى لِي أَبْكِي وَأُنْشِدُ وَأَقُولُ هَذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ —
sentences.tr: bi-rūḥī wa-dakhaltu al-ḥammāma qabla an akhruja min al-baliyyati wa-ḥalaqtu dhaqnī wa-labistu misḥan aswada wa-ḥaṭṭaytu ʿalā raʾsī bā sīdī wa-fī kulli yawmin abkī wa-aftakiru al-maṣāʾiba allatī jarat ʿalayya wa-qalʿa ʿaynī wa-kulla mā aftakiru jarā lī abkī wa-unshidu wa-aqūlu hādhihi al-abyāta —
sentences.l: With my soul (barely saved) I entered the bath before I went out from the calamity, and I shaved my chin, and I put on a black felt(-garment) and set upon my head [a] bā-sīdī, and every day I weep and recall the calamities that befell me and the gouging-out of my eye; and whenever I recall (what happened) to me I weep and recite and say these verses —
sentences.i: With my life barely spared, I went into the bath-house before I quitted that place of ruin; there I shaved my chin, put on a garment of black felt, and set upon my head a [mourning cap of some kind]. And every day I would weep and dwell upon the misfortunes that had befallen me and the gouging-out of my eye; and whenever I recalled what had happened to me, I would weep, and recite, and speak these verses —
sentences.n: 'بروحي' continues the idiom 'خرج بروحه' — to escape a danger 'with one's (bare) life/soul,' i.e. barely alive. 'با سيدي' (P102L02) is left only lightly vocalised: it is an obscure dialectal item, most plausibly the name of a mourning head-covering (a felt cap or turban-wrap) worn with the black mourning felt just mentioned, but its exact lexical identity cannot be established with confidence from the text alone, so no definite gloss is offered beyond 'a kind of cap.' 'قلع عيني' is taken as a second, coordinate object of 'أفتكر' alongside 'المصائب' (i.e. 'I recall the calamities... and the gouging-out of my eye'), hence its accusative marking.

sentences.t:
تَحَيَّرْتُ وَالرَّحْمَنِ لَا شَكَّ فِي أَمْرِي * وَحَالَتْ بِيَ الْأَحْزَانُ مِنْ حَيْثُ لَا أَدْرِي
سَأَصْبِرُ حَتَّى يَعْجِزَ الصَّبْرُ مِنْ صَبْرِي * وَأَصْبِرُ حَتَّى يَقْضِيَ اللَّهُ مِنْ أَمْرِي
سَأَصْبِرُ مَغْلُوبًا وَلَمْ أَتَوَجَّعْ * كَمَا يَصْبِرُ الظَّمْآنُ فِي الْوَادِي الْحَرِّ
سَأَصْبِرُ حَتَّى يَعْلَمَ الصَّبْرُ أَنَّنِي * صَبَرْتُ عَلَى شَيْءٍ أَمَرَّ مِنَ الصَّبْرِ
وَلَا شَيْءَ مِثْلَ الصَّبْرِ مُرٌّ وَإِنَّمَا * أَمَرُّ مِنَ الْأَمْرَيْنِ أَنْ خَانَنِي صَبْرِي
سَرَائِرُ سِرِّي تُرْجُمَانُ سَرِيرَتِي * إِذَا كَانَ سِرُّ السِّرِّ سِرُّكَ فِي سِرِّي
وَلَوْ أَنَّ مَا بِي لِلْجِبَالِ لَهَدَمَتْ * وَبِالنَّارِ أَطْفَاهَا وَبِالرِّيحِ لَمْ تَسْرِي
وَمَنْ قَالَ إِنَّ الدَّهْرَ فِيهِ حَلَاوَةٌ * فَلَا بُدَّ مِنْ يَوْمٍ أَمَرَّ مِنَ الصَّبْرِ
sentences.tr:
taḥayyartu wa-al-raḥmani lā shakka fī amrī * wa-ḥālat biya al-aḥzānu min ḥaythu lā adrī
sa-aṣbiru ḥattā yaʿjiza al-ṣabru min ṣabrī * wa-aṣbiru ḥattā yaqḍiya allāhu min amrī
sa-aṣbiru maghlūban wa-lam atawajjaʿ * ka-mā yaṣbiru al-ẕamʾānu fī al-wādī al-ḥarri
sa-aṣbiru ḥattā yaʿlama al-ṣabru annanī * ṣabartu ʿalā shayʾin amarra mina al-ṣabri
wa-lā shayʾa mithla al-ṣabri murrun wa-innamā * amarru mina al-amrayni an khānanī ṣabrī
sarāʾiru sirrī turjumānu sarīratī * idhā kāna sirru al-sirri sirruka fī sirrī
wa-law anna mā bī li-al-jibāli la-hadamat * wa-bi-al-nāri aṭfāhā wa-bi-al-rīḥi lam tasrī
wa-man qāla inna al-dahra fīhi ḥalāwatun * fa-lā budda min yawmin amarra mina al-ṣabri
sentences.l:
Bewildered am I — by the Merciful, there is no doubt of my case — // and sorrows have come over me from whence I do not know
I shall be patient till patience itself is worn out by my patience // and I shall be patient till God accomplishes my affair
I shall be patient, overcome, and not complain of pain, // as the thirsty man is patient in the hot valley
I shall be patient till Patience itself knows that I // have borne a thing more bitter than patience
And nothing is like patience (in being) bitter, and yet // more bitter than the two bitter things is that my patience betrayed me
The secrets of my secret are the interpreter of my inmost self; // if the secret of the secret is your secret, (it is) within my secret
And if what is in me befell the mountains, it would have levelled them, // and with fire it would have quenched it, and with wind it would not have travelled
And whoever says that time holds any sweetness — // there must needs be a day more bitter than patience
sentences.i:
Bewildered am I — by the Merciful God, there is no doubt of my case — // and grief has closed upon me from a quarter I cannot know.
I will endure until endurance itself is outworn by my endurance, // and I will bear on until God brings my affair to its end.
Vanquished, I will endure, and utter no complaint, // even as the thirsting man endures within the scorching valley.
I will endure until Patience herself must own // that I have borne a thing more bitter than patience.
Nothing is so bitter as patience — and yet // more bitter still, of the two bitternesses, is that my own patience failed me.
The secrets within my secret are the voice of my hidden heart; // if the secret of secrets is your secret, it lies within my secret.
Had what afflicts me fallen upon the mountains, it would have brought them down; // fire could not have quenched it, nor could the wind have swept it on.
And whoever claims that Time holds any sweetness — // let him know: a day must come more bitter than patience itself.
sentences.n: A vow-of-endurance poem built on repeated دّهُ صَبْر/صَبَرَ ('patience/to be patient') across six of the eight lines, with a triple play on سِرّ ('secret') in line 6. In context this is not an inserted love-lyric but the mutilated Qalandar's own oath to bear his fate, though its diction (bewilderment, betrayal, an addressed 'you' in the secret-couplet) is the conventional amatory/gnomic register often used at emotional turns in this text. Every verse word above is copied exactly as marked in the archive; nothing in the verse was vocalised by the editor.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ سَافَرْتُ الْاَقْطَارَ وَوَرَدْتُ الْاَمْصَارَ وَقَصَدْتُ دَارَ السَّلَامِ بَغْدَادَ لَعَلِّي اَتَوَصَّلُ اِلَى اَمِيرِ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ وَاُخْبِرُهُ بِمَا جَرَى لِي
sentences.tr: thumma sāfartu al-aqṭāra wa-waradtu al-amṣāra wa-qaṣadtu dāra al-salāmi baghdāda laʿallī atawaṣṣalu ilā amīri al-muʾminīna wa-ukhbiruhu bi-mā jarā lī
sentences.l: Then I traveled the regions, and I entered the cities, and I made for the Abode of Peace, Baghdad, so that perhaps I gain access to the Commander of the Believers and inform him of what had happened to me,
sentences.i: Then I traveled through the lands and entered the cities, making for Baghdad, the Abode of Peace, hoping I might reach the Commander of the Faithful and tell him what had befallen me,
sentences.n: اقطار and امصار are broken plurals of the pattern أَفْعَال, which begins with hamzat al-qaṭʿ; the edition prints the seat bare, so the hamza is supplied as a combining mark rather than the precomposed أ.

sentences.t: فَوَصَلْتُ بَغْدَادَ هٰذِهِ اللَّيْلَةَ فَوَجَدْتُ اَخِي هٰذَا الْاَوَّلَ وَاقِفًا حَائِرًا فَقُلْتُ السَّلَامُ عَلَيْكَ وَ تَحَدَّثْتُ مَعَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-waṣaltu baghdāda hādhihi al-laylata fa-wajadtu akhī hādhā al-awwala wāqifan ḥāʾiran fa-qultu al-salāmu ʿalayka wa-taḥaddathtu maʿahu
sentences.l: so I arrived in Baghdad this (very) night, and I found this my brother, the first, standing, bewildered, and I said, "Peace (be) upon you," and I conversed with him,
sentences.i: and so I arrived in Baghdad that very night, and found this brother of mine, the first, standing there bewildered; I said, "Peace be upon you," and fell to talking with him,
sentences.n: هٰذَا / هٰذِهِ are given the traditional dagger-alif spelling used in fully-pointed Classical texts: the bare rasm is only three letters (ه ذ ا / ه ذ ه), and the dagger alif simply marks the unwritten first vowel, so stripping it returns exactly the edition's bare spelling.

sentences.t: وَاِذَا بِاَخِينَا الثَّالِثِ قَدْ اَقْبَلَ عَلَيْنَا وَقَالَ السَّلَامُ عَلَيْكُمْ اَنَا رَجُلٌ غَرِيبٌ
sentences.tr: wa-idhā bi-akhīnā al-thālithi qad aqbala ʿalaynā wa-qāla al-salāmu ʿalaykum anā rajulun gharībun
sentences.l: and suddenly, there was our third brother, having come upon us, and he said, "Peace be upon you (pl.); I (am) a strange man,"
sentences.i: and all at once our third brother appeared before us and said, "Peace be upon you; I am a stranger,"
sentences.n: بِـ after اذا of surprise only marks what suddenly appears ("and lo, with our brother..." = "and lo, there was our brother"); it adds no meaning of its own here.

sentences.t: فَقُلْنَا لَهُ وَنَحْنُ غُرَبَاءُ وَقَدْ وَصَلْنَا هٰذِهِ اللَّيْلَةَ الْمُبَارَكَةَ
sentences.tr: fa-qulnā lahu wa-naḥnu ghurabāʾu wa-qad waṣalnā hādhihi al-laylata al-mubārakata
sentences.l: so we said to him, "And we (are) strangers, and we have (already) arrived this blessed night,"
sentences.i: so we told him, "We too are strangers, and we arrived only this very blessed night,"

sentences.t: فَتَمَشَّيْنَا نَحْنُ الثَّلَاثَةُ وَمَا فِينَا اَحَدٌ يَعْرِفُ حِكَايَةَ اَحَدٍ فَسَاقَتْنَا الْمَقَادِيرُ اِلَى هٰذَا الْبَابِ وَدَخَلْنَا اِلَيْكُمْ
sentences.tr: fa-tamashshaynā naḥnu al-thalāthatu wa-mā fīnā aḥadun yaʿrifu ḥikāyata aḥadin fa-sāqatnā al-maqādīru ilā hādhā al-bābi wa-dakhalnā ilaykum
sentences.l: so we walked along, we three, and there was not among us anyone who knew another's tale, and the decrees (of fate) drove us to this door, and we entered in unto you,
sentences.i: so we three walked on together, and none of us knew the others' stories, until the decrees of fate drove us to this very door, and we came in to you,

sentences.t: وَهٰذَا سَبَبُ حَلْقِ ذَقْنِي وَشَوَارِبِي وَ قَلْعِ عَيْنِي
sentences.tr: wa-hādhā sababu ḥalqi dhaqnī wa-shawāribī wa-qalʿi ʿaynī
sentences.l: and this (is) the cause of the shaving of my chin and my mustaches and the plucking-out of my eye,
sentences.i: and this is the reason my chin and mustaches were shaved and my eye put out,

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ اِنَّ حِكَايَتَكَ غَرِيبَةٌ مَلِّسْ عَلَى رَاسِكَ وَاخْرُجْ اِلَى حَالِ سَبِيلِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat inna ḥikāyataka gharībatun mallis ʿalā rāsika wa-akhruj ilā ḥāli sabīlika
sentences.l: so she said, "Indeed your tale is strange; slip off (with your hand) over your head, and go out to the state of your way,"
sentences.i: so she said, "Truly your tale is strange; count yourself lucky and be on your way,"
sentences.n: مَلِّسْ عَلَى رَاسِكَ ("slip/stroke over your head") is a colloquial Middle-Arabic idiom of dismissal, roughly "make yourself scarce" or "be content and go" — not a Classical construction. The imperative مَلِّسْ (form II of a colloquial root م-ل-س, "to slip away") is vocalised as printed rather than emended to a Classical verb.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَا اَخْرُجُ حَتَّى اَسْمَعَ حَدِيثَ رِفْقَتِي
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lā akhruju ḥattā asmaʿa ḥadītha rifqatī
sentences.l: so he said, "I will not go out until I hear the account of my companions,"
sentences.n: The identical consonants اخرج carry two different hamzas within two lines: as the form-I imperative in the sentence above (اِخْرُجْ) it is the elidable hamzat al-waṣl and takes no hamza-mark; here, as the 1st-person present tense (اَخْرُجُ), the initial hamza is a true hamzat al-qaṭʿ, so it is marked with the combining hamza above.

sentences.t: فَتَقَدَّمَ الْقَرَنْدَلِيُّ الثَّالِثُ وَقَالَ اَيَّهَا السِّتُّ الْجَلِيلَةُ مَا قِصَّتِي مِثْلَ قِصَّتِهِمْ بَلْ قِصَّتِي اَعْجَبُ وَاَغْرَبُ
sentences.tr: fa-taqaddama al-qarandalīyu al-thālithu wa-qāla ayyahā al-sittu al-jalīlatu mā qiṣṣatī mithla qiṣṣatihim bal qiṣṣatī aʿjabu wa-aghrabu
sentences.l: then the third qalandar came forward and said, "O the lady, the noble one, my story (is) not like their story; rather my story (is) more wondrous and stranger,"
sentences.i: then the third qalandar stepped forward and said, "O noble lady, my story is not like theirs; mine is stranger still, and more amazing,"
sentences.n: ايها is the masculine vocative particle, used here invariantly even though the person addressed (السّت, "the lady") is feminine, where Classical grammar would call for أَيَّتُهَا. The text does not make the distinction, so it is vocalised اَيَّهَا rather than silently corrected.

sentences.t: وَهِيَ سَبَبٌ لِحَلْقِ ذَقْنِي وَقَلْعِ عَيْنِي اِنَّ هٰؤُلَاءِ جَاءَهُمُ الْقَضَا وَالْقَدَرُ وَاَنَا جَلَبْتُ الْقَضَاءَ بِيَدِي وَالْهَمَّ لِرُوحِي
sentences.tr: wa-hiya sababun li-ḥalqi dhaqnī wa-qalʿi ʿaynī inna hāʾulāʾi jāʾahumu al-qaḍā wa-al-qadaru wa-anā jalabtu al-qaḍāʾa bi-yadī wa-al-hamma li-rūḥī
sentences.l: and it (is) a cause for the shaving of my chin and the plucking-out of my eye: indeed, to these (others), fate and destiny came (on their own), but I, I drew destiny (upon myself) by my (own) hand, and the grief for my (own) soul,
sentences.i: and that is the cause of my chin's shaving and my eye's loss: fate and destiny simply came upon those other men, but I brought destiny down on myself with my own hand, and grief upon my own soul,
sentences.n: The text spells "fate" two different ways within one breath: القضا without the final hamza-letter (a common defective Middle-Arabic spelling, kept as printed) and, a few words later, القضاء with the hamza written out; both are vocalised for the same word qaḍāʾ. هٰؤُلَاءِ: the source spells the medial hamza-seat as a bare و rather than the expected ؤ, so the combining hamza above is added to it, while the final ء is already given precomposed in the source and kept as is.

sentences.t: وَذٰلِكَ اَنِّي كُنْتُ مَلِكًا ابْنَ مَلِكٍ وَمَاتَ وَالِدِي وَاَخَذْتُ الْمُلْكَ مِنْ بَعْدِهِ وَ حَكَمْتُ وَعَدَلْتُ وَاَحْسَنْتُ لِلرَّعِيَّةِ
sentences.tr: wa-dhālika annī kuntu malikan ibna malikin wa-māta wālidī wa-akhadhtu al-mulka min baʿdihi wa-ḥakamtu wa-ʿadaltu wa-aḥsantu li-al-raʿīyati
sentences.l: and that (is) that I was a king, son of a king, and my father died, and I took the kingship after him, and I ruled, and I was just, and I did good to the subjects,
sentences.i: and it was this: I was a king, son of a king; my father died, and I took the throne after him, and I ruled with justice and dealt well with my subjects,

sentences.t: وَكَانَ لِي مَحَبَّةٌ فِي السَّفَرِ فِي الْمَرْكَبِ فِي الْبَحْرِ وَكٰنَتْ مَدِينَتِي عَلَى الْبَحْرِ وَالْبَحْرُ مُتَّسِعٌ وَحَوْلَنَا جَزَائِرُ كَثِيرَةٌ عَظِيمَةٌ فِي وَسَطِ الْبَحْرِ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna lī maḥabbatun fī al-safari fī al-markabi fī al-baḥri wa-kānat madīnatī ʿalā al-baḥri wa-al-baḥru muttasiʿun wa-ḥawlanā jazāʾiru kathīratun ʿaẕīmatun fī wasaṭi al-baḥri
sentences.l: and I had a love of traveling by ship on the sea, and my city was upon the sea, and the sea (was) vast, and around us (were) many great islands in the middle of the sea,
sentences.i: I had a passion for traveling the sea by ship; my city stood upon the sea, a vast sea ringed with many great islands,
sentences.n: The text spells "was" (fem., agreeing with مدينتي) with the same three letters as كنت ("I was", 1st person) — كنت for كانت — omitting the medial alif. It is pointed كٰنَتْ with a dagger alif, on the same principle as قل for قال, rather than read as the 1st person.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ لِي فِي الْبَحْرِ خَمْسُونَ مَرْكَبًا لِلْمَتْجَرِ وَخَمْسُونَ مَرْكَبًا اَصْغَرُ لِلْفُرْجَةِ وَمِائَةٌ وَخَمْسُونَ قِطْعَةً مُعَدَّةً لِلْحَرْبِ وَالْجِهَادِ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna lī fī al-baḥri khamsūna markaban li-al-matjari wa-khamsūna markaban aṣghara li-al-furjati wa-miʾatun wa-khamsūna qiṭʿatan muʿaddatan li-al-ḥarbi wa-al-jihādi
sentences.l: and I had upon the sea fifty ships for trade, and fifty smaller ships for pleasure-outings, and a hundred and fifty vessels made ready for war and combat,
sentences.i: on the sea I kept fifty ships for trade, fifty smaller ones for pleasure cruises, and a hundred and fifty vessels fitted out for war,

sentences.t: فَاَرَدْتُ اَنْ اَتَفَرَّجَ عَلَى الْجَزَائِرِ فَنَزَلْتُ فِي عَشَرَةِ مَرَاكِبَ وَاَخَذْتُ مَعِي زَادَ شَهْرٍ كَامِلٍ وَسَافَرْتُ عِشْرِينَ يَوْمًا
sentences.tr: fa-aradtu an atafarraja ʿalā al-jazāʾiri fa-nazaltu fī ʿasharati marākiba wa-akhadhtu maʿī zāda shahrin kāmilin wa-sāfartu ʿishrīna yawman
sentences.l: so I wished that I might go about looking at the islands, so I went down into ten ships, and I took with me the provisions of a whole month, and I traveled twenty days,
sentences.i: so, wishing to go touring the islands, I embarked on ten ships, took with me a full month's provisions, and set sail for twenty days,

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتْ لَيْلَةٌ مِنَ اللَّيَالِي هَبَّتْ عَلَيْنَا رِيَاحٌ مُخْتَلِفَةٌ وَهَاجَ الْبَحْرُ عَلَيْنَا هَيَجَاتٍ عَظِيمَةٍ وَتَلَاطَمَتِ الْاَمْوَاجُ فَاَيِسْنَا مِنَ الْحَيَوةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānat laylatun min al-layālī habbat ʿalaynā riyāḥun mukhtalifatun wa-hāja al-baḥru ʿalaynā hayajātin ʿaẕīmatin wa-talāṭamati al-amwāju fa-ayisnā min al-ḥayawati
sentences.l: then, when it was a night among the nights, contrary winds blew upon us, and the sea surged against us with mighty surgings, and the waves dashed against each other, and we despaired of life,
sentences.i: then, one night, contrary winds beat upon us, and the sea heaved with tremendous swells and the waves crashed together, until we despaired of life,
sentences.n: فايسنا: the source spells "we despaired" with no hamza-letter at all (ف ا ي س ن ا), pointing to the rarer metathesis-variant root أَيِسَ (beside the more common يَئِسَ); the combining hamza above is supplied on the initial alif accordingly. الحيوة keeps the old orthography with wāw standing for the final ā (compare صلوة for صلاة), kept as printed and read ḥayāh.

sentences.t: وَنَزَلَتْ عَلَيْنَا ظُلْمَةٌ شَدِيدَةٌ وَقُلْتُ لَيْسَ الْمُخَاطِرُ بِمَحْمُودٍ وَلَوْ سَلِمَ
sentences.tr: wa-nazalat ʿalaynā ẕulmatun shadīdatun wa-qultu laysa al-mukhāṭiru bi-maḥmūdin wa-law salima
sentences.l: and a heavy darkness came down upon us, and I said, "The risk-taker is not praiseworthy, even if he comes through safe,"
sentences.i: and a heavy darkness settled over us, and I said, "Even a lucky gamble is no credit to the gambler,"
sentences.n: بِمَحْمُودٍ: the بِـ here is the بِـ that regularly marks the predicate of the negating verb لَيْسَ ("is not X"), not an independent preposition of place or instrument.

sentences.t: فَدَعَوْنَا اللّٰهَ تَعَالَى وَابْتَهَلْنَا اِلَيْهِ وَلَا زَالَتِ الْاَرْيَاحُ تَخْتَلِفُ وَالْاَمْوَاجُ تَلْتَطِمُ اِلَى اَنْ انْفَجَرَ الْفَجْرُ
sentences.tr: fa-daʿawnā allāha taʿālā wa-ibtahalnā ilayhi wa-lā zālat al-aryāḥu takhtalifu wa-al-amwāju taltaṭimu ilā an infajara al-fajru
sentences.l: so we called upon God, may He be exalted, and we implored Him, and the winds did not cease to vary, and the waves to dash against each other, until the dawn broke,
sentences.i: so we called upon God the Exalted and prayed to Him fervently, while the winds kept changing and the waves kept crashing, until at last the dawn broke,
sentences.n: الارياح: this plural has an extra alif not found in the more usual رياح (used two sentences earlier for the same word), suggesting the rarer pattern أَرْيَاح, parallel to أَمْوَاج; vocalised with hamzat al-qaṭʿ rather than silently normalised to رياح.

sentences.t: فَهَدَتِ الرِّيحُ وَصَفَا الْبَحْرُ وَبَعْدَهُ اَشْرَقَتِ الشَّمْسُ
sentences.tr: fa-hadati al-rīḥu wa-ṣafā al-baḥru wa-baʿdahu ashraqati al-shamsu
sentences.l: then the wind grew still, and the sea became clear, and after it the sun rose,
sentences.n: هَدَتِ is written with no hamza-letter at all, where Classical spelling would have هَدَأَتْ (root هدأ, "to grow calm"); the hamza consonant has simply dropped from the spelling, a Middle-Arabic simplification kept as printed rather than restored.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ اَنَّنَا اَشْرَفْنَا عَلَى جَزِيرَةٍ وَطَلَعْنَا عَلَى الْبَرِّ وَطَبَخْنَا شَيْئًا نَأْكُلُهُ فَاَكَلْنَا ثُمَّ اَخَذْنَا رَاحَةَ يَوْمَيْنِ وَسَافَرْنَا عِشْرِينَ يَوْمًا
sentences.tr: thumma annanā ashrafnā ʿalā jazīratin wa-ṭalaʿnā ʿalā al-barri wa-ṭabakhnā shayʾan nākuluhu fa-akalnā thumma akhadhnā rāḥata yawmayni wa-sāfarnā ʿishrīna yawman
sentences.l: then we came in sight of an island, and we went up onto the shore, and we cooked something (that) we might eat it, and we ate; then we took the rest of two days, and we traveled twenty days,
sentences.i: then an island came into view, and we went ashore and cooked something to eat, and ate; then we rested two days and sailed on for twenty more,
sentences.n: نَأْكُلُهُ is printed with the hamza already precomposed (نأكله) in the source and kept as given, while فاكلنا two words later, for the very same root, is printed with a bare alif and so takes the combining hamza above (فَاَكَلْنَا) — the edition is simply inconsistent between the two spellings.

sentences.t: فَاخْتَلَفَتْ عَلَيْنَا الْمِيَاهُ وَعَلَى الرَّئِسِ وَاسْتَغْرَبَ الرَّئِسُ الْبَحْرَ
sentences.tr: fa-ikhtalafat ʿalaynā al-miyāhu wa-ʿalā al-raʾisi wa-istaghraba al-raʾisu al-baḥra
sentences.l: then the waters grew strange upon us and upon the captain, and the captain found the sea strange,
sentences.i: then the waters turned strange on us and on the captain, and the captain himself found the sea grown strange,
sentences.n: الرئس: a defective spelling of الرئيس ("the captain"), dropping the ي of the -īs syllable while keeping the hamza-seat ئ; read al-raʾīs throughout. It is the same word as "chief, president" in modern usage, but here means specifically the ship's captain.

sentences.t: فَقُلْنَا لِلنَّاظُورِ اُكْشُفِ الْبَحْرَ وَاُطْلُعِ الْبِطِّيَّةَ فَطَلَعَ الْمَسَارِي
sentences.tr: fa-qulnā li-al-nāẕūri ukshufi al-baḥra wa-uṭluʿi al-biṭṭīyata fa-ṭalaʿa al-masārī
sentences.l: so we said to the lookout, "Scan the sea, and go up (to) the look-out post," so he climbed the mast-ropes,
sentences.i: so we told the lookout, "Search the sea, and get up to the crow's nest," and he swarmed up the rigging,
sentences.n: البِطِّيَّة and المَسَارِي are uncertain nautical terms — probably the masthead look-out post and the mast's ropes/rigging, respectively — and are vocalised only lightly, since neither the exact reading nor the precise technical sense can be established with confidence; المساري may simply be a plural of سارِيَة, "mast".

sentences.t: ثُمَّ نَظَرَ النَّاظُورُ وَقَالَ لِلرَّئِسِ
sentences.tr: thumma naẕara al-nāẕūru wa-qāla li-al-raʾisi
sentences.l: then the lookout looked, and he said to the captain—

sentences.t: يَا رَئِسُ رَأَيْتُ عَنْ يَمِينِي سَمَكً عَلَى وَجْهِ الْمَاءِ وَنَظَرْتُ إِلَى وَسَطِ الْبَحْرِ فَرَأَيْتُ سَوَادًا مِنْ بَعِيدٍ يَلُوحُ سَاعَةً أَسْوَدَ وَسَاعَةً أَبْيَضَ
sentences.tr: yā raʾisu raʾaytu ʿan yamīnī samakan ʿalā wajhi al-māʾi wa-naẓartu ilā wasaṭi al-baḥri fa-raʾaytu sawādan min baʿīdin yalūḥu sāʿatan aswada wa-sāʿatan abyaḍa
sentences.l: O captain, I saw, to my right, fish upon the face of the water, and I looked toward the middle of the sea, and I saw a blackness from afar, gleaming — one moment black and one moment white.
sentences.i: O captain, I saw fish to my right on the surface of the water, and when I looked out toward the middle of the sea I saw a dark shape far off, flickering, now black, now white.
sentences.n: رئس is a defective spelling of الرئيس 'captain,' with the internal يـ of the pattern فَعِيل simply omitted — a common economy of this manuscript's Middle Arabic, also seen just above in سمك, whose accusative tanwīn (samakan) is written without the usual supporting alif (سمكً rather than سمكًا). Both are vocalised and read as the fuller Classical forms though the rasm itself is shorter.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ الرَّئِسُ كَلَامَ النَّاظُورِ ضَرَبَ عِمَامَتَهُ فِي الْأَرْضِ وَنَتَفَ لِحْيَتَهُ وَقَالَ لِلنَّاسِ أَبْشِرُوا بِهَلَاكِنَا نَحْنُ الْجَمِيعُ وَلَمْ يَسْلَمْ مِنَّا أَحَدٌ وَ شَرَعَ يَبْكِي وَنَحْنُ الْجَمِيعُ نَبْكِي عَلَى أَنْفُسِنَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa al-raʾisu kalāma al-nāẓūri ḍaraba ʿimāmatahu fī al-arḍi wa-natafa liḥyatahu wa-qāla li-al-nāsi abshirū bi-halākinā naḥnu al-jamīʿu wa-lam yaslam minnā aḥadun wa-sharaʿa yabkī wa-naḥnu al-jamīʿu nabkī ʿalā anfusinā
sentences.l: So when the captain heard the lookout's words, he threw his turban to the ground and tore at his beard, and said to the crew, 'Receive the glad-tidings of our destruction, all of us — not one of us shall be saved!' — and he began to weep, and we, all of us, wept over ourselves.
sentences.i: When the captain heard what the lookout said, he flung his turban down and tore at his beard, crying to the crew, 'Brace yourselves — we are all doomed, and not one of us will escape!' Then he broke into weeping, and all of us wept for ourselves.
